name: Square Georges-Cain

beats.script_body: Square Georges-Cain opened in 1931, tucked behind the Carnavalet museum on rue de Sévigné in the heart of Marais museum country. At its center is a circular garden featuring a bronze sculpture called Dawn. The benches facing the garden are the favored preserve of Parisians reading Le Monde or basking in silence under a pale sun. In late spring the square is surrounded on all sides by a profusion of blooming rosebushes.

beats.script_body: Square Georges-Cain doubles as an archaeological depository for stone fragments salvaged from older gardens — including the Tuileries. Scattered among the greenery are pieces of an older Paris, rescued and quietly preserved in this hidden corner of the Marais.

beats.script_body: The square takes its name from Georges Cain (1856–1919), a painter and writer who served as the first curator of the Carnavalet museum — the institution whose back wall forms the square's eastern border. Cain's double identity as artist and museum guardian is embodied in this quiet corner of the Marais that still bears his name.

beats.script_body: Along the square's north perimeter runs the seventeenth-century Orangerie of the Hôtel le Peletier de Saint-Fargeau — the mansion at a right angle to the Carnavalet. Both mansions are linked together by a long gallery. The ensemble creates the sheltered walls of this quiet square, making it one of the most architecturally distinguished of Parisian pocket gardens.

name: Square Léopold-Achille

beats.script_body: The large Parc Royal that once occupied this ground was the royal menagerie of Francis I, who raised camels and ostriches here — and who gave the street its name, rue du Parc Royal. Today the space is Square Léopold-Achille, a lawn crowded with reclining families on Sunday afternoons, children playing football outside the railings in front of Café Sévigné.

name: Clos des Blancs-Manteaux

beats.script_body: At 21, rue des Blancs-Manteaux — a street Jean-Paul Sartre wrote a song about — sits the Clos des Blancs-Manteaux, a small enclosed garden of biodiversité with 250 varieties of plants. The garden is dedicated to the memory of Princess Diana, who died in Paris on August 31, 1997. It is only open on weekends; during the week the surrounding buildings house a day-care center and preschool.

name: Square du Temple
short_description: Public garden on the site of the Knights Templar fortress, later the prison of the Royal Family during the Revolution

beats.script_body: In 1140, this site became the headquarters of the Knights Templar — a hugely wealthy and propertied international religious order established to protect pilgrims to Jerusalem. The Templars' territory included large swaths of land in the northern and southern Marais. Their fortress was a towering castle inhabited by thousands of monk-soldiers, with a prison at the center of the enclosure. The Templars also acted as bankers to financially stressed kings, hiding them on occasion from rioting mobs.

beats.source_passage: In 1140, the site became the headquarters of the Knights Templar, a hugely wealthy and propertied international religious order established to protect pilgrims to Jerusalem. The Templars' territory included large swaths of land in the northern and southern Marais. Their fortress, a towering castle, was inhabited by thousands of monk-soldiers; in the center of the enclosure was the prison. The Templars acted as bankers to financially stressed kings, hiding them on occasion from rioting mobs.

beats.script_body: In 1307, in need of cash, the savage Philippe le Bel — he was good-looking — declared war on the Templars. Charging them with heresy, sodomy, and necromancy, he invaded, razed, arrested, tortured, and burned at the stake the monks who would not confess. Among those executed was Jacques Molay, the Father General: he was hung from the scaffold and burned alive near the Square Vert Galant.

flagged_claims.claim: Jacques Molay burned alive near the Square Vert Galant
flagged_claims.notes: Historical sources agree Molay was burned on the Île de la Cité, near what is now Square du Vert-Galant, in March 1314. This is consistent with Cahill. However she states he 'was hung from the scaffold and burned alive' — most sources say burned at the stake directly, not hanged. Flag for fact-check.

beats.script_body: Louis XVI, Marie-Antoinette, the dauphin — Louis XVII — and his sister were imprisoned in the same Temple keep where the Templars had been tortured, before the king and queen went to the guillotine in 1793. The dauphin was held for another three years, when he died. Napoleon, afraid the site would become a destination of royalist pilgrims, had the prison razed.

beats.script_body: Today there's a large sign in the square bearing the names of the youngest children — unrecorded in school registers — who were deported by the Nazis from the Marais homes bordering the square. Once the property of the incinerated Templars, the neighborhood had become home to Jewish artisans and merchants.

beats.script_body: At the rue de Bretagne entrance there's a lovely rock garden and pond with a small waterfall — another triumph of the engineer and landscape architect John-Charles Adolphe Alphand. All along the paths the gardens are planted with spirea, lilacs, and flowering fruit trees. Near the western edge you pass the sculpted head of the poet and songwriter Béranger, the French Robert Burns, whose socialist sympathies and lyrics landed him in jail in the nineteenth century.

beats.script_body: On a quiet Sunday morning — sleepy fathers minding toddlers, solitaries sitting under the apple trees deep in newspapers — it would never cross your mind that Square du Temple has been eyewitness to carnage, conflagration, torture, regicide, genocide, eight centuries of atrocities buried alive in Parisian memory.

name: Marche des Enfants Rouges
short_description: Oldest covered market in Paris established in 1615, named after a nearby orphanage where children wore red cloaks

beats.script_body: The Marché des Enfants Rouges is the oldest covered food market in Paris. It is named for an orphanage founded on this site by Francis I: the orphans wore red. The narrow entrance is off rue de Bretagne and rue Charlot.

judgement_basis: A narrow covered market with fragile stalls and produce at child height where running is unsafe and unwelcome, whose only seating is paid food-stall benches, and which is gated and locked outside market hours leaving nowhere lit to stand at night.
queue_basis: A covered public market with open entrances and no admission control, so visitors walk straight in and there is no line to enter.

name: Musee des Arts et Metiers
short_description: Science and technology museum founded in 1794 with 80,000 objects including Foucault's original pendulum in a medieval chapel
name_variations: Conservatoire National des Arts et Metiers

beats.script_body: On the south side of the Musée des Arts et Métiers, along the ancient rue Saint-Martin — passing Saint-Martin des Champs and Saint-Nicolas des Champs — lies the small Square E. Chautemps, under chestnut trees. A Wallace fountain — a symbol of Parisian parks and squares — faces the Conservatoire.
